editorial: Perhaps our expectations were coloured by its currency being the Euro, but Greece was surprisingly affordable. Athens was especially cheap compared to Istanbul, which was interesting considering Greece’s higher per capita incomes.

categories.title: STAYS
editorial: Our four nights cost $435, with the beautiful Anafi suite in Santorini accounting for $135 per night (which by the way, is par for the course in the Aegean islands).
Athens was much cheaper at $82 a night in a residential building only 10 minutes from the Acropolis.

categories.title: FOOD
editorial: Gyros at local legend Kostas in Athens cost $3, whereas the rolls at Istanbul’s equivalent, Durumzade, cost twice as much.
Even the fanciest lunch we had in Santorini (at Melitini) was about $70 for two.

categories.title: EXPERIENCES
editorial: Our mythology tour of ancient Athens was $65 per person plus a $20 tip. Additionally, we paid $50 each for entrance to the Acropolis and the Agora.
Unfortunately, we were underwhelmed by the tour. We’d mention the tour operator, but those details aren’t mentioned on our receipts!

categories.title: INTER-CITY TRAVELS
editorial: We forked out $365 to Volotea airlines, including an unnecessary $60 fine, for the honour of flying us to Santorini.
It’s mostly low-cost airlines operating this route, so if you’re not pressed for time, take the boat.

categories.title: MISCELLANEOUS
editorial: Our visas cost about $90 each. We spent in the range of $20 on moving around the island of Santorini. We walked all across Athens.

alternatives.title: What if we had a bigger budget?
editorial: We’d splurge more in Santorini stay. We would choose a fancier property closer to the caldera and town rather than upgrading anything in Athens.

alternatives.title: What if we had a smaller budget?
editorial: Take the ferry from Athens to Santorini. If we did, it would’ve saved us $300 (and a lot of anguish).
